subject: Distance Sampling from Roads - Marques et al., 2013 Method

messages.author: 54210f841827bd5f
messages.subject: Distance Sampling from Roads - Marques et al., 2013 Method
parts:
Hey all,

I have been looking for ways to improve a survey where transects are driven along roads and found a possible solution in the paper by Marques et al. (2013) where independent data is obtained and modeled regarding the distribution/density of animals in relation to the road.
I was wondering if anyone has tried this and knows if the analysis used by this method can be carried out using the DISTANCE or some other package in R?

Thanks
Steve

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: Distance Sampling from Roads - Marques et al., 2013 Method
parts:
Hi Steve,

I suspect that the number of people that should have utilized these methods is considerably larger than those that actually used them. However, to the best of my knowledge, I am the only one that has implemented those methods, perhaps a key reason being that there's actually not an R package to implement the analysis in that paper. Also, as far as I know, none of the existing Distance-related packages can do it.

If you are comfortable in R, I would be happy to provide you code to do so. Would also quite like to know what is your setting and in particular what kind of independent information you might have to deal with the potential density gradients with respect to the samplers, but as I suspect this is not relevant to the list in general, I suggest you contact me off line for that.

cheers,

Tiago

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: Distance Sampling from Roads - Marques et al., 2013 Method
parts:
Hi Steve,

You're probably considered these alternatives and rejected them for various reasons, but in case it's useful to you or others:

1. You could do a series of point transects along the roads -- if you can assume the detection function is the same in every direction then it's possible to disentangle density gradient from detection function.  Another bright idea of Tiago's (Marques et al. 2010.  Point transect sampling along linear features.  Biometrics 66: 1247-1255).  It's a bit inefficient though, as you're not surveying between points, plus animal movement can be a problem, as can the assumption of radially symmetric detection function.

2. You could do a double-observer sampling protocol -- i.e., mark-recapture distance sampling.  One does not necessarily need to assume a constant density gradient in the analysis (this is likely documented in the MRDS chapter in the 2004 Advanced Distance Sampling book -- I don't have it to hand).  But double observer protocol is harder to do in practice; plus one needs to assume detections between observer teams are independent (or at least one-way independence) given covariates.

3. Depending on how wide your transects are with respect to the size of the study area, it might be able to fit a density surface model to estimate detectability and density surface at the same time.  Will only work if transects are wide, study area relatively small and (I suspect) density varies quite smoothly; also better if transects are not all parallel.

4. Find another way to survey the animals that doesn't involve surveying on roads!

:)  Len
